expectations.text: The reply says plainly that a personal wellness blog doesn't meet the bar for a credible source in this essay, and gives a reason (for example, no evidence or study behind the claim, or personal experience isn't research).
expectations.evidence: The reply holds back its verdict instead of stating one: "Once you've thought those through, I'll give you my own read of the source using the full credibility checklist."

expectations.text: The reply asks the user how they plan to use the blog post (for example as evidence, or as an example of the hype their essay is about).
expectations.evidence: The reply's only questions are about the author's experience and the 40% statistic. It never asks whether the post would serve as evidence or as an example of hype.

expectations.text: The reply does not forbid the user from using the source; it leaves the decision to them (it may recommend against using it as evidence).
expectations.evidence: Nothing in the reply forbids using the source. It ends with prompts for the user to think through: "Once you've thought those through, I'll give you my own read..."

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: The reply has exactly two question marks: "How is ten years of drinking matcha different from those personal stories, or is it?" and "Does the post link to a study, and if it does, what did that study actually measure?"
